subject: Cooking
title: The Gluten-Free Boom: Science vs. Trend
description: A quick, practical guide to The Gluten-Free Boom: Science vs. Trend.

hook.text: 30% of Americans actively avoid gluten. Only 1% have celiac disease. What's going on?

buildup.text: Non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS) may affect 6% of people — real symptoms, but no autoimmune damage.

discovery.text: Some researchers believe FODMAPs — fermentable carbs in wheat — cause symptoms blamed on gluten.

twist.text: Blinded studies show many self-diagnosed 'gluten sensitive' people can't distinguish gluten from placebo.

climax.text: The $7.5 billion gluten-free market thrives on a mix of real need and powerful marketing.

punchline.text: Gluten is a real problem for some. A perceived one for many.

quiz.question: What might cause symptoms often blamed on gluten in non-celiac individuals?

details.summary: The gluten-free market exceeded $7 billion despite only one percent of people having celiac disease. Many adopt gluten-free diets without medical necessity, driven by celebrity endorsements and wellness marketing.
details.whyItMatters: The gluten-free trend illustrates how health marketing can outrun science. Distinguishing genuine celiac disease from trend-driven avoidance matters for both health and food culture.
takeaways: Gluten-free market exceeds $7 billion, mostly non-celiac buyers
Blinded studies fail to confirm most self-reported sensitivity
Unnecessary avoidance can reduce fiber and nutrient intake

faq.question: Do most people benefit from going gluten-free?
faq.answer: People with celiac disease absolutely must avoid gluten. For the general population, rigorous studies show no health benefit. Gluten-free products often contain more sugar, fat, and additives to compensate for texture changes.

faq.question: Why do some people feel better after going gluten-free?
faq.answer: Eliminating gluten often means eating fewer processed foods, more vegetables, and paying more attention to diet — all of which improve how people feel. The nocebo effect plays a role in self-diagnosed sensitivity. Some may actually be sensitive to FODMAPs in wheat rather than gluten itself.
